title: Chapter 4: Consumer and Producer Surplus, Market Efficiency, and Welfare

questions.title: Defining Individual Consumer Surplus
questions.prompt_template: In microeconomics, how is an individual buyer's consumer surplus on a single purchased unit defined?

hints.text: Think about the gap between the highest price a shopper would pay before walking away and the actual price charged at the register.
Recall the definition of willingness to pay (WTP) relative to the market price paid.

options_template.text: The difference between the buyer's maximum willingness to pay and the actual market price paid.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Consumer surplus measures the net benefit a buyer captures when the market price is below their maximum willingness to pay (CS = WTP - P).

options_template.text: The total dollar amount the buyer actually spends at checkout for the unit.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Expenditure Confusion): The amount spent at checkout is total consumer expenditure (P x Q), not the net surplus gained over what the buyer paid.

options_template.text: The difference between the market price paid and the seller's marginal production cost.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Producer-Side Reversal): Market price minus marginal cost defines producer surplus, not consumer surplus.

options_template.text: The total quantity of units a shopper buys before their budget reaches zero.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Budget-Constraint Confusion): Consumer surplus is measured in dollars of net value above price paid, not as a physical count of units purchased.

questions.title: Intramarginal Units versus the Marginal Unit
questions.prompt_template: When a rational consumer buys multiple cups of coffee at a constant market price of $4 per cup, why does the final (marginal) cup purchased yield zero additional consumer surplus?

hints.text: Compare the consumer's personal valuation of their first cup versus the very last cup they decide to buy.
Ask what happens if the buyer's willingness to pay for the next cup is strictly above $4 versus strictly below $4.

options_template.text: Because the coffee shop charges a higher price for the last cup than for the first cup.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Variable-Price Assumption): In a competitive single-price market, every cup sells at the same market price of $4; the difference lies in declining marginal willingness to pay.

options_template.text: Because for the last unit bought, the buyer's marginal willingness to pay just equals the market price of $4.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Buyers keep purchasing additional units as long as WTP >= P; they stop at the marginal unit where WTP = P, leaving $4 - $4 = $0 in extra surplus on that last unit.

options_template.text: Because total consumer surplus across all cups purchased must always equal zero in equilibrium.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Total vs. Marginal Confusion): Only the marginal (last) unit yields zero extra surplus; intramarginal (earlier) units with WTP > $4 still generate positive total consumer surplus.

options_template.text: Because the marginal cost of brewing the last cup drops to zero once fixed costs are paid.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Supply-Side Substitution): Consumer surplus depends on the buyer's willingness to pay relative to price, not on the seller's fixed-cost structure.

questions.title: The Choke Price and Marshall's Axis Convention
questions.prompt_template: On a standard linear market demand diagram with price on the vertical axis and quantity on the horizontal axis, what does the vertical intercept (choke price) represent?

hints.text: Substitute Q = 0 into a linear inverse demand equation such as P = 100 - 2Q.
Interpret what a quantity demanded of zero means for buyers' willingness to pay.

options_template.text: The lowest price at which firms are willing to begin producing output.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Supply-Intercept Confusion): The lowest price at which sellers enter the market is the vertical intercept of the supply curve (P_min), not the demand curve.

options_template.text: The equilibrium price at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Equilibrium Confusion): Equilibrium occurs where the demand and supply curves intersect at a positive quantity, not at Q = 0.

options_template.text: The price threshold at or above which quantity demanded falls to zero because no buyer is willing to purchase the good.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Found by setting Q = 0 in the inverse demand curve, the choke price is the upper valuation boundary where no consumer is willing to buy even a single unit.

options_template.text: The maximum physical quantity consumers would take if the good were given away for free.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Horizontal-Intercept Confusion): Quantity demanded when P = 0 is the horizontal (quantity) intercept, not the vertical (price) intercept.

questions.title: Willingness to Accept and Marginal Cost
questions.prompt_template: In a competitive market, what economic concept directly determines a seller's minimum willingness to accept (WTA) for producing and selling one additional unit of output?

hints.text: Consider what extra cost a firm incurs specifically because it chooses to produce one more unit.
Contrast incremental operating costs with fixed overhead expenses that must be paid regardless of output.

options_template.text: The firm's monthly fixed rent divided equally across all units sold.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Average-Fixed-Cost Confusion): Fixed overhead like rent does not change when one more unit is produced and therefore does not determine the marginal willingness to accept.

options_template.text: The highest willingness to pay among consumers in the market.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Demand-Side Substitution): Consumer willingness to pay determines the demand curve, whereas seller willingness to accept is grounded in production cost.

options_template.text: The firm's historical total revenue from the previous fiscal year.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Sunk-History Fallacy): Past revenue does not determine the minimum price needed to justify producing an additional unit today.

options_template.text: The marginal cost of producing that additional unit.
options_template.feedback: Correct. A seller will only produce and sell an extra unit if the market price at least covers the direct extra cost of making it, so WTA equals marginal cost (MC).

questions.title: Producer Surplus versus Accounting Profit
questions.prompt_template: Why is a firm's producer surplus generally larger than its accounting profit in the short run?

hints.text: Write out the formulas for Producer Surplus and Profit in terms of Total Revenue, Total Variable Cost, and Total Fixed Cost.
Identify which cost category is subtracted when calculating profit but omitted when calculating producer surplus.

options_template.text: Producer surplus equals Total Revenue minus Total Variable Cost, whereas profit also subtracts Total Fixed Costs such as rent and insurance.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Because PS = TR - TVC and Profit = TR - TVC - TFC = PS - TFC, producer surplus represents operating cash flow before fixed overhead is deducted.

options_template.text: Producer surplus includes government subsidies, whereas accounting profit excludes all tax and subsidy flows.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Subsidy Attribution Error): Even in a market with no subsidies, producer surplus exceeds profit whenever positive fixed costs exist.

options_template.text: Producer surplus subtracts only fixed costs from total revenue and ignores all variable input costs.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Cost-Category Inversion): Producer surplus subtracts variable production costs (the area under the MC/supply curve), not fixed costs.

options_template.text: Producer surplus measures revenue per unit, whereas accounting profit measures revenue across all units sold.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Unit-vs-Total Confusion): Both total producer surplus and total profit are aggregate dollar figures summed across all units sold.

questions.title: Why Intramarginal Units Generate Larger Producer Surplus
questions.prompt_template: Along an upward-sloping supply curve in a competitive market, why do the earliest units produced generate more producer surplus per unit than the final unit sold at equilibrium?

hints.text: Think about why the supply curve slopes upward as firms expand output.
Compare the vertical gap between P* and MC at low quantities versus at Q*.

options_template.text: Early units are sold to wealthier buyers at higher prices than later units.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Price-Discrimination Assumption): In a single-price competitive market, all units sell at the same equilibrium price P*; the changing element is marginal cost.

options_template.text: Diminishing returns cause marginal cost to rise with output, so early units are produced more cheaply while the final unit breaks even on operating cost (P* = MC).
options_template.feedback: Correct. Earlier intramarginal units have low marginal cost relative to P*, generating large surplus per unit, whereas rising marginal cost shrinks per-unit surplus to zero at the marginal unit.

options_template.text: Fixed costs apply only to the final unit produced, reducing its net surplus to zero.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Fixed-Cost Allocation Error): Fixed costs do not vary with output and do not enter marginal cost or per-unit producer surplus.

options_template.text: Sellers intentionally lower product quality on later units, forcing the market price down.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Quality-Variation Fallacy): Standard supply models assume homogeneous units sold at a single equilibrium price P*.

questions.title: Why Market Price Cancels Out in Total Social Surplus
questions.prompt_template: In the equation Total Social Surplus = Consumer Surplus + Producer Surplus, what economic role does the market price play?

hints.text: For any single traded unit, add (WTP - P) and (P - MC) algebraically.
Notice what happens to P in that sum, and ask what P still determines between the two sides of the market.

options_template.text: A higher market price automatically increases total social surplus because sellers receive more money.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Producer-Only Accounting): Any dollar gained by a seller from a higher price on a traded unit is an exact dollar lost by the buyer, leaving their sum unchanged for that unit.

options_template.text: A lower market price automatically maximizes total social surplus regardless of whether sellers produce the good.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Consumer-Only Accounting): Lowering price below equilibrium transfers surplus on traded units to buyers, but reduces quantity supplied and shrinks total surplus via deadweight loss.

options_template.text: Price cancels out in the sum for each traded unit, so price divides the economic pie between buyers and sellers while the volume of mutually beneficial trades determines the pie's size.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Because (WTP - P) + (P - MC) = WTP - MC, the transfer price P determines how surplus is split, whereas the quantity of trades with WTP >= MC determines total welfare.

options_template.text: Price determines total social surplus only when the supply curve is completely horizontal.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Special-Case Misattribution): The algebraic cancellation of P inside CS + PS holds for every traded unit regardless of the slope of supply or demand.

questions.title: Allocative Efficiency and Pareto Efficiency
questions.prompt_template: Which condition characterizes an allocatively and Pareto efficient competitive market equilibrium?

hints.text: Compare society's marginal benefit (height of demand) with society's marginal cost (height of supply) at Q*.
Recall the definition of Pareto efficiency regarding whether anyone can be made better off without harming someone else.

options_template.text: Consumer surplus is guaranteed to be strictly equal to producer surplus.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Equal-Split Fallacy): CS and PS only happen to be equal when supply and demand have equal slope magnitudes; efficiency maximizes CS + PS regardless of their split.

options_template.text: Every consumer who wants the good receives it at a price of zero.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Zero-Price Fallacy): Producing units whose marginal cost exceeds buyers' marginal benefit destroys social surplus.

options_template.text: Firms earn zero producer surplus so that all gains from trade go strictly to consumers.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Zero-PS Confusion): Maximizing total surplus requires compensating sellers at least their marginal cost; along an upward-sloping supply curve, efficient markets generate positive PS.

options_template.text: Marginal benefit equals marginal cost (MB = MC), maximizing total surplus so no one can be made better off without making someone else worse off.
options_template.feedback: Correct. At Q* where MB = MC, every trade with WTP >= MC takes place and no trade with MC > WTP occurs, achieving both allocative efficiency and Pareto efficiency.

questions.title: Binding versus Non-Binding Price Ceilings
questions.prompt_template: When is a legally mandated price ceiling considered binding in a competitive market?

hints.text: Remember that a price ceiling sets a legal maximum price above which sellers may not legally charge.
Compare the legal maximum price to the unregulated market equilibrium price P*.

options_template.text: Only when the legal maximum price is set strictly below the natural equilibrium price, preventing the market from clearing and creating a shortage.
options_template.feedback: Correct. A price ceiling binds when P_bar < P*, forcing price below equilibrium so quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied.

options_template.text: Only when the legal maximum price is set strictly above the natural equilibrium price, creating a surplus of unsold inventory.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Ceiling-Floor Reversal): A legal maximum set above P* is non-binding (the market naturally settles at P*); a legal minimum set above P* is a binding price floor.

options_template.text: Whenever the government announces a maximum price, regardless of where equilibrium lies.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Legal-Status Fallacy): A ceiling set above P* does not constrain market transactions because the equilibrium price is already legally permissible.

options_template.text: Only when quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded at the regulated price.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Surplus-Shortage Inversion): A binding price ceiling depresses price below equilibrium, causing a shortage (Q_d > Q_s), never a surplus.

questions.title: The Short-Side Rule and Deadweight Loss under a Price Ceiling
questions.prompt_template: Under a binding price ceiling where quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied, what determines the actual number of units traded in the market, and why does deadweight loss arise?

hints.text: Think about how many transactions can occur when 30 buyers want a good but sellers only produce 10 units.
Connect the missing units between Q_s and Q* to trades where willingness to pay exceeded marginal cost.

options_template.text: Actual trades equal quantity demanded because buyers legally force sellers to meet all requests, creating zero deadweight loss.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Forced-Supply Fallacy): Sellers cannot be compelled to produce units at a loss below marginal cost; voluntary exchange is capped by the smaller side.

options_template.text: Actual trades equal the smaller of quantity supplied and quantity demanded (Q_s), blocking mutually beneficial trades between Q_s and Q* and generating deadweight loss.
options_template.feedback: Correct. By the short-side rule, Q_actual = min(Q_s, Q_d) = Q_s; units from Q_s to Q* had WTP > MC but are never produced, permanently destroying social surplus.

options_template.text: Actual trades equal the midpoint average of quantity demanded and quantity supplied, eliminating half of the shortage.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Midpoint-Averaging Fallacy): Markets do not average Q_d and Q_s when price cannot adjust; transactions cannot exceed the quantity actually supplied.

options_template.text: Actual trades remain unchanged at Q*, and deadweight loss equals the dollar transfer from producers to consumers.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Transfer-vs-DWL Confusion): A binding ceiling reduces quantity to Q_s < Q*, and pure transfers between buyers and sellers are not deadweight loss—only lost mutually beneficial trades are.

questions.title: Anatomy of an Excise Tax Wedge
questions.prompt_template: What is the fundamental effect of levying a per-unit excise tax of t dollars on a competitive market?

hints.text: Distinguish between the total price paid by the buyer (P_buyer) and the net price kept by the seller (P_seller).
Write the equation relating P_buyer, P_seller, and t.

options_template.text: It forces buyers and sellers to pay the exact same price while increasing equilibrium quantity traded.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Zero-Wedge Fallacy): An excise tax separates the buyer's price from the seller's net price and contracts, rather than expands, market output.

options_template.text: It transfers 100% of total social surplus directly to the government as tax revenue.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Total-Confiscation Fallacy): Buyers and sellers still retain positive post-tax CS and PS on remaining units, while lost trades become deadweight loss that nobody receives.

options_template.text: It drives a tax wedge (P_buyer - P_seller = t) between what buyers pay and what sellers keep, reducing market output below Q*.
options_template.feedback: Correct. An excise tax inserts a vertical gap of t dollars between buyer price and seller net price, discouraging marginal trades so Q_t < Q*.

options_template.text: It creates a permanent physical shortage identical to a binding price ceiling.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Tax-Ceiling Conflation): Unlike a price ceiling, prices adjust under an excise tax so quantity demanded at P_buyer equals quantity supplied at P_seller—no physical shortage occurs.

questions.title: Statutory Incidence versus Economic Incidence
questions.prompt_template: According to the Statutory Neutrality principle for excise taxes, what is the difference between statutory incidence and economic incidence?

hints.text: Compare who is legally required to remit the tax check to the government with who actually suffers the price change in the market.
Recall the Chapter 4 proof comparing Case A (tax collected from sellers) and Case B (tax collected from buyers).

options_template.text: Statutory incidence determines who bears the financial burden, while economic incidence only measures government revenue.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Incidence Reversal): Economic incidence—not statutory incidence—measures how the true financial burden is shared between buyers and sellers.

options_template.text: When a tax is legally levied on sellers, sellers always bear 100% of the economic burden.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Statutory-Literalism Fallacy): Sellers shift part of the tax to buyers through a higher market price; legal assignment does not dictate economic burden.

options_template.text: Statutory incidence applies only to price ceilings, while economic incidence applies only to excise taxes.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Policy-Scope Error): Both statutory and economic incidence are core concepts of tax analysis.

options_template.text: Statutory incidence specifies who legally remits the tax to the government, whereas economic incidence measures the true financial burden—and final P_buyer, P_seller, and Q_t are identical regardless of statutory assignment.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Shifting supply up by t or shifting demand down by t creates the exact same tax wedge, post-tax quantity, buyer price, and seller net price.

questions.title: The Quadratic Excess Burden Theorem
questions.prompt_template: In a market with linear supply and demand curves, what does the Quadratic Excess Burden Theorem state about how deadweight loss responds when a per-unit excise tax rate t is doubled (assuming positive output remains)?

hints.text: Recall the Harberger triangle formula DWL = (1/2) * t * Delta Q, where Delta Q itself is proportional to t.
Substitute Delta Q = t / (b + d) into the DWL formula to see how DWL depends on t.

options_template.text: Deadweight loss quadruples because DWL grows with the square of the tax rate (DWL proportional to t^2).
options_template.feedback: Correct. Doubling t doubles both the vertical height (t) and horizontal base (Delta Q) of the Harberger triangle, multiplying its area by 2 x 2 = 4.

options_template.text: Deadweight loss exactly doubles because DWL grows linearly in proportion to the tax rate.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Linear-Scaling Fallacy): Students often forget that raising t increases both the tax wedge and the quantity contraction simultaneously, causing quadratic—not linear—growth.

options_template.text: Deadweight loss remains unchanged because only government tax revenue changes when t rises.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Constant-DWL Fallacy): A larger tax wedge prices additional mutually beneficial trades out of the market, expanding the Harberger triangle.

options_template.text: Deadweight loss falls by half because fewer units are left in the market to distort.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Shrinkage Inversion): Having fewer units traded means more trades were destroyed (larger Delta Q), which makes deadweight loss strictly larger, not smaller.

questions.title: Locating Consumer Surplus on a Market Diagram
questions.prompt_template: On a standard supply-and-demand coordinate graph in equilibrium at (Q*, P*), which geometric region represents Total Consumer Surplus?

hints.text: For each unit from 0 to Q*, consumer surplus is the vertical gap from the market price line up to the demand curve.
Identify the three boundaries enclosing that shaded triangle.

options_template.text: The rectangle enclosed below the equilibrium price line P* and to the left of Q*.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Expenditure-Rectangle Confusion): The rectangle P* x Q* represents total consumer spending (and firm revenue), not consumer surplus.

options_template.text: The triangle bounded below the demand curve, above the horizontal equilibrium price line P*, from Q = 0 to Q*.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Consumer surplus sums WTP - P* across all units from 0 to Q*, forming the triangle beneath demand and above P*.

options_template.text: The triangle bounded above the supply curve and below the horizontal equilibrium price line P*, from Q = 0 to Q*.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Producer-Surplus Swap): The region above the supply curve and below P* represents Producer Surplus, not Consumer Surplus.

options_template.text: The entire area beneath the demand curve from Q = 0 to Q*, all the way down to the horizontal quantity axis.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Gross-vs-Net Benefit Confusion): The entire area under demand down to the axis measures gross willingness to pay (total benefit); you must subtract expenditure P* x Q* to get net consumer surplus.

questions.title: Effect of a Rightward Supply Shift on Consumer Surplus
questions.prompt_template: Suppose a breakthrough in shipping technology shifts the market supply curve to the right while the demand curve remains unchanged. How does the shaded Consumer Surplus triangle on the graph change?

hints.text: Trace the movement from the old equilibrium along the stationary downward-sloping demand curve.
Observe what happens to both the height (P_choke - P*) and the base (Q*) of the consumer surplus triangle.

options_template.text: It shrinks because lower prices reduce the value consumers place on the product.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Price-Value Conflation): A lower market price does not lower consumers' willingness to pay (the demand curve stays fixed); it increases the gap WTP - P*.

options_template.text: It stays constant in area because the gain in quantity is exactly offset by the drop in price.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Revenue-vs-Surplus Confusion): While total expenditure P* x Q* can rise or fall, both the height (P_choke - P*) and base (Q*) of the CS triangle increase, so CS strictly expands.

options_template.text: It expands both vertically and horizontally because existing buyers pay a lower price and new buyers enter as equilibrium quantity rises.
options_template.feedback: Correct. A lower P* increases the height (P_choke - P*) and increases the base Q*, strictly enlarging the consumer surplus triangle.

options_template.text: It shifts entirely to the right without changing size because the demand curve did not move.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Static-Triangle Error): Even when the demand curve is stationary, moving downward along it to a lower P* and higher Q* enlarges the triangle beneath it.

questions.title: Comparing Vertical Gaps Along a Demand Curve
questions.prompt_template: On a downward-sloping linear demand curve with equilibrium at Q* = 20 and P* = $60, how does the vertical height between the demand curve and the price line at Q = 5 compare to the vertical height at Q = 20?

hints.text: Measure the vertical distance from the horizontal line P* = $60 up to the demand curve at Q = 5 versus at Q = 20.
Remember that at Q* = 20, the demand curve intersects the horizontal line P* = $60.

options_template.text: Both vertical heights are equal to $60 because every consumer pays the same market price.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Constant-Surplus Fallacy): Although every buyer pays $60, buyers' willingness to pay declines as Q moves rightward, so surplus per unit is not constant.

options_template.text: The vertical height is smaller at Q = 5 than at Q = 20 because fewer units have been sold.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Horizontal-Vertical Reversal): A smaller Q sits higher on a downward-sloping demand curve, producing a larger vertical gap above P*.

options_template.text: The vertical height is negative at Q = 5 and positive at Q = 20.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Sign-Inversion Error): All units from 0 to Q* have WTP >= P*, so their vertical gaps above P* are non-negative.

options_template.text: The vertical height is strictly positive at Q = 5 (representing intramarginal surplus) and shrinks to zero at Q = 20 (the marginal unit).
options_template.feedback: Correct. At Q = 5 the demand curve lies well above $60, yielding positive surplus, whereas at Q* = 20 the demand curve touches $60, giving zero surplus on the marginal unit.

questions.title: Locating Producer Surplus on a Market Diagram
questions.prompt_template: On a standard linear supply-and-demand diagram in equilibrium at (Q*, P*), which geometric region corresponds to Total Producer Surplus?

hints.text: For every unit from 0 to Q*, producer surplus is the vertical gap from the supply (marginal cost) curve up to the market price P*.
Check which triangle sits below the price line P* and above the upward-sloping supply curve.

options_template.text: The triangle located above the upward-sloping supply curve and below the equilibrium price line P*, from Q = 0 to Q*.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Summing (P* - MC) across all units from 0 to Q* forms the triangle above supply and below the market price line.

options_template.text: The trapezoid located beneath the upward-sloping supply curve down to the horizontal axis, from Q = 0 to Q*.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Variable-Cost Confusion): The area underneath the supply (marginal cost) curve from 0 to Q* represents Total Variable Cost, not Producer Surplus.

options_template.text: The triangle located below the demand curve and above the equilibrium price line P*, from Q = 0 to Q*.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Consumer-Surplus Swap): The triangle below demand and above P* measures Consumer Surplus, not Producer Surplus.

options_template.text: The entire rectangle of width Q* and height P*.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Revenue-vs-Surplus Confusion): The rectangle P* x Q* is Total Revenue; you must subtract Total Variable Cost (area under supply) to isolate Producer Surplus.

questions.title: Effect of a Rightward Demand Shift on Producer Surplus
questions.prompt_template: Suppose consumer demand for tutoring surges, shifting the market demand curve to the right while the upward-sloping supply curve stays fixed. What happens visually to the Producer Surplus triangle?

hints.text: Identify the new equilibrium point along the stationary upward-sloping supply curve.
Examine how the higher P* and higher Q* change both the height (P* - P_min) and base (Q*) of the Producer Surplus triangle.

options_template.text: It shrinks because sellers must incur higher marginal costs to produce extra units.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Marginal-Cost Tunnel Vision): While marginal cost rises on newly added units, P* rises above MC for all existing units and new units also earn positive surplus, so total PS grows.

options_template.text: It expands because existing sellers earn a higher price on original units and additional units enter the market above their marginal cost.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Moving up along the stationary supply curve raises both P* and Q*, enlarging the Producer Surplus triangle vertically and horizontally.

options_template.text: It remains unchanged because the supply curve itself did not shift.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Curve-Shift Fixation): Producer surplus depends on P* and Q*, so a demand-driven movement along a stationary supply curve directly changes PS.

options_template.text: It disappears completely because marginal cost equals price at the new equilibrium.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Marginal-vs-Total Confusion): Price equals marginal cost only on the final unit Q*; all earlier units still earn P* > MC, generating a larger total Producer Surplus.

questions.title: Interpreting the Supply Vertical Intercept P_min
questions.prompt_template: On a linear supply graph P = 20 + 2Q, the vertical intercept is P_min = $20. What does this point indicate graphically, and what happens to P_min if variable input costs fall by $5 per unit?

hints.text: Set Q = 0 to see what P_min means for firms' willingness to enter production.
Think about how a $5 drop in marginal cost shifts the supply curve vertically.

options_template.text: P_min = $20 is the maximum price sellers can charge, and lower input costs raise it to $25.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Choke-Price Inversion): $20 is the minimum price required to elicit any supply, and lower input costs reduce—not raise—that threshold.

options_template.text: P_min = $20 is the equilibrium price, and lower input costs leave it fixed at $20.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Equilibrium-Intercept Confusion): The vertical intercept is evaluated at Q = 0, whereas equilibrium occurs where supply intersects demand at Q* > 0.

options_template.text: Below $20 no seller is willing to supply a unit, and a $5 drop in per-unit variable cost shifts the supply curve downward so P_min falls to $15.
options_template.feedback: Correct. P_min is the minimum supply threshold at Q = 0; lowering marginal cost by $5 shifts the supply curve down by $5, reducing P_min from $20 to $15.

options_template.text: Below $20 sellers earn zero fixed costs, and lower variable costs shift the supply curve upward to $25.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Shift-Direction Reversal): Lower production costs increase supply, which shifts the supply curve downward/rightward, not upward/leftward.

questions.title: Why Underproduction (Q < Q*) Reduces Total Social Surplus
questions.prompt_template: Suppose a market is restricted to producing a quantity Q_1 strictly below its competitive equilibrium Q*. Graphically, why is Total Social Surplus strictly smaller at Q_1 than at Q*?

hints.text: Compare the height of the demand curve to the height of the supply curve for every unit between Q_1 and Q*.
Visualize the triangular gap sitting between the two curves from Q_1 to Q*.

options_template.text: Because for units between Q_1 and Q*, the supply curve lies above the demand curve, so halting output prevents losses.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Left-Right Side Reversal): To the left of Q* (Q < Q*), the demand curve lies above the supply curve (MB > MC), meaning those unproduced units would have created positive gains from trade.

options_template.text: Because cutting output below Q* shifts the demand curve inward toward the origin.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Movement-vs-Shift Confusion): Restricting quantity does not shift underlying consumer preferences (demand); it leaves mutually beneficial units unproduced.

options_template.text: Because total surplus is always proportional to equilibrium price, which falls when Q < Q*.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Price-Maximizer Fallacy): Total surplus is the area between demand and supply over traded units, not the level of price.

options_template.text: Because for every unit between Q_1 and Q*, demand lies above supply (WTP > MC), so failing to produce those units leaves a triangle of mutually beneficial gains uncaptured.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Stopping at Q_1 < Q* forfeits the triangle between demand and supply from Q_1 to Q*, creating deadweight loss.

questions.title: Why Overproduction (Q > Q*) Creates Deadweight Loss
questions.prompt_template: If a government mandate forced firms to produce and sell a quantity Q_2 strictly greater than the competitive equilibrium Q*, what would the graph reveal about the units between Q* and Q_2?

hints.text: Look to the right of the equilibrium intersection E*(Q*, P*) and compare the heights of the supply and demand curves.
Determine whether marginal benefit exceeds marginal cost or marginal cost exceeds marginal benefit for units beyond Q*.

options_template.text: The supply curve lies above the demand curve (MC > MB), meaning those extra units cost society more to produce than buyers value them, creating a deadweight loss triangle to the right of E*.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Beyond Q*, marginal cost exceeds marginal willingness to pay (P_s > P_d), so each additional unit destroys social welfare, forming a negative-surplus DWL triangle to the right of E*.

options_template.text: Total social surplus continues to grow because producing more physical goods always increases societal welfare.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (More-Is-Always-Better Fallacy): Producing units whose resource cost exceeds consumer valuation wastes scarce resources and shrinks net social welfare.

options_template.text: The demand curve remains above the supply curve beyond Q*, so consumer surplus expands without bound.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Curve-Crossing Error): Past the equilibrium intersection E*, the upward-sloping supply curve rises above the downward-sloping demand curve.

options_template.text: Deadweight loss is zero because every unit produced is eventually consumed.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Zero-Waste Assumption): Consuming a unit that cost $80 in resources to produce when the buyer values it at only $40 creates a $40 net loss to society.

questions.title: Reading Shortage and Deadweight Loss on a Price Ceiling Graph
questions.prompt_template: On a graph showing a binding price ceiling set below P* (such as P_bar = $40 when P* = $60), how are the physical shortage and the deadweight loss triangle identified visually?

hints.text: Locate Q_s where the horizontal ceiling line hits the supply curve and Q_d where it hits the demand curve.
Notice that the shortage is a horizontal distance along the ceiling line, whereas deadweight loss is a triangle between Q_s and Q*.

options_template.text: The shortage is the vertical distance P* - P_bar, and the DWL triangle spans horizontally from Q* to Q_d.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Axis-Swap & Wrong-Side Triangle): Shortage is a horizontal quantity gap (Q_d - Q_s), not a vertical price gap, and DWL lies between Q_s and Q* where trades were lost.

options_template.text: The shortage is the horizontal gap Q_d - Q_s along the ceiling line, and the DWL triangle lies between demand and supply from Q_s to Q*.
options_template.feedback: Correct. The horizontal gap from Q_s to Q_d measures excess demand (shortage), while the triangle bounded by demand, supply, and the vertical line at Q_s represents lost gains from trade.

options_template.text: The shortage is the horizontal gap Q* - Q_s, and the DWL triangle is the entire area under demand between Q_s and Q_d.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Lost-Output-vs-Shortage Confusion): Q* - Q_s is the drop in output, which is only part of the shortage Q_d - Q_s (since Q_d also rises above Q*).

options_template.text: Both the shortage and the DWL triangle disappear once the ceiling line is drawn below P_min.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Extreme-Ceiling Error): Setting a ceiling below P_min eliminates all production (Q_s = 0), maximizing both the shortage and deadweight loss.

questions.title: Graphical Outcome of a Non-Binding Price Ceiling
questions.prompt_template: In a market with equilibrium price P* = $60 and quantity Q* = 20, the city passes a law imposing a price ceiling at $75. What happens on the supply-and-demand graph?

hints.text: Draw a horizontal line at P = $75 and check whether the free-market price of $60 violates the legal maximum.
Remember that a price ceiling prohibits charging MORE than the ceiling, not LESS.

options_template.text: Price rises to $75, creating a surplus because quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded at $75.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Ceiling-as-Floor Confusion): A price ceiling is a maximum price, not a minimum price; sellers do not raise price to $75 when the market already clears legally at $60.

options_template.text: Price falls to $45 to maintain symmetry around equilibrium, creating a deadweight loss triangle.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Symmetry Fabrication): A legal maximum above equilibrium imposes no constraint on market pricing.

options_template.text: The ceiling is non-binding, so the market remains at E*(20, $60) with unchanged CS, unchanged PS, and zero deadweight loss.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Because $60 is already legally below the $75 maximum, the ceiling has no effect on price, quantity, or social welfare.

options_template.text: Quantity demanded collapses to zero because $75 exceeds buyers' willingness to pay.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Ceiling-as-Actual-Price Fallacy): Buyers still pay the market equilibrium price of $60, not the $75 legal cap.

questions.title: Graphical Equivalence of Taxing Sellers versus Taxing Buyers
questions.prompt_template: Compare two graphs of the exact same market subjected to a $12 excise tax: Graph A shifts the supply curve vertically upward by $12 (tax on sellers), while Graph B shifts the demand curve vertically downward by $12 (tax on buyers). How do the resulting tax wedges compare?

hints.text: In Graph A, read P_b at the new intersection and drop down $12 to the original supply curve for P_s.
In Graph B, read P_s at the new intersection and rise up $12 to the original demand curve for P_b.

options_template.text: Graph A produces a higher P_b and lower Q_t than Graph B because sellers pass the full $12 onto buyers.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Asymmetric-Pass-Through Fallacy): Both shifts insert the exact same $12 vertical wedge between original demand and original supply, yielding identical Q_t and prices.

options_template.text: Graph B produces a larger deadweight loss triangle because shifting demand reduces buyers' willingness to pay.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (WTP-Shift Confusion): Underlying consumer valuation of the good is unchanged; only the net price buyers can offer the seller drops by $12, yielding the exact same Harberger triangle.

options_template.text: Graph A generates government revenue, whereas Graph B eliminates government revenue because buyers remit the tax directly.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Collection-Channel Fallacy): In both cases, government collects t x Q_t = $12 x Q_t in tax revenue.

options_template.text: Both graphs produce the exact same post-tax quantity Q_t, buyer price P_b, seller net price P_s, tax revenue box, and deadweight loss triangle.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Regardless of which curve shifts, the tax wedge fits at the identical quantity Q_t where P_d(Q_t) - P_s(Q_t) = $12, proving statutory neutrality graphically.

questions.title: Distinguishing Tax Revenue from Deadweight Loss on a Tax Wedge Graph
questions.prompt_template: On a supply-and-demand diagram showing an excise tax of t dollars that reduces quantity from Q* to Q_t, how do the shapes representing Government Tax Revenue and Deadweight Loss differ?

hints.text: Tax revenue is collected only on the units still sold (from 0 to Q_t), while deadweight loss occurs on the units no longer sold (from Q_t to Q*).
Identify the rectangle versus the triangle formed by the tax wedge t.

options_template.text: Government tax revenue is the rectangle of width Q_t and height t (from Q = 0 to Q_t), while deadweight loss is the Harberger triangle between demand and supply from Q_t to Q*.
options_template.feedback: Correct. The government collects t on every unit from 0 to Q_t (area t x Q_t), while lost trades from Q_t to Q* form the DWL triangle of area (1/2) x t x (Q* - Q_t).

options_template.text: Government tax revenue is the triangle from Q_t to Q*, while deadweight loss is the rectangle from 0 to Q_t.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Shape-Identity Inversion): Revenue is the rectangle on traded units (t x Q_t), whereas DWL is the Harberger triangle on eliminated units.

options_template.text: Government tax revenue is the rectangle of width Q* and height t, which already includes the deadweight loss triangle.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Pre-Tax-Base Fallacy): The government cannot collect tax on units between Q_t and Q* that are never bought or sold.

options_template.text: Both government tax revenue and deadweight loss are triangles that sit entirely above the equilibrium price P*.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Buyer-Side-Only Distortion): Both the revenue box and the Harberger triangle straddle P*—spanning vertically from P_s below P* up to P_b above P*.

questions.title: Asymmetric Slopes and Economic Tax Incidence
questions.prompt_template: Consider a market where the demand curve is visibly much steeper (more inelastic) than the relatively flat (more elastic) supply curve. When a per-unit excise tax t is fitted as a vertical wedge between the curves, what does the graph show about the division of the tax burden?

hints.text: Compare the vertical rise in buyer price (P_b - P*) above the old equilibrium line to the vertical drop in seller net price (P* - P_s) below it.
Remember that along a steeper curve, a small drop in quantity causes a large vertical change in price.

options_template.text: Buyers and sellers still split the tax 50/50 because the tax wedge is a single vertical segment.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Always-50/50 Fallacy): A 50/50 split occurs only when supply and demand have equal slope magnitudes; asymmetric slopes produce unequal burdens.

options_template.text: Buyers bear a larger share of the tax burden (P_b - P* > P* - P_s) because the steeper demand curve rises sharply as quantity contracts.
options_template.feedback: Correct. The less elastic (steeper) side of the market has fewer alternatives to avoid the tax, so moving left from Q* to Q_t pushes P_b up much more than it pushes P_s down.

options_template.text: Sellers bear a larger share of the tax burden (P* - P_s > P_b - P*) because a flatter supply curve drops faster as quantity falls.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Slope-Incidence Reversal): Moving left along a flat curve causes only a small price drop; the steeper—not flatter—curve absorbs the larger price swing.

options_template.text: Deadweight loss becomes infinite because buyers refuse to adjust their quantity.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Inelastic-DWL Confusion): Steeper (more inelastic) demand causes a smaller contraction in quantity (Delta Q), which actually results in a smaller—not larger—deadweight loss.

questions.title: Calculating Total Consumer Surplus for Four Discrete Buyers
questions.prompt_template: Four students each consider buying one concert ticket. Their maximum willingness to pay (WTP) is $85 for Maya, $70 for Devon, $55 for Priya, and $40 for Luis. If the market price of a ticket is $50, what is the total consumer surplus across all four students?

hints.text: First determine which students actually buy a ticket (those with WTP >= $50) and which student walks away empty-handed.
Compute (WTP - $50) for each purchasing student and add those individual surpluses together.

options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Negative-Surplus Inclusion): Including Luis ($40 - $50 = -$10) erroneously assumes a rational buyer pays $50 for a ticket they value at $40. Luis does not buy, contributing $0 surplus.
Diagnostic fallacy (Gross-WTP Summation): $85 + $70 + $55 = $210 sums the buyers' total willingness to pay without subtracting the $50 ticket price paid by each of the three buyers.
Correct. Maya ($85 - $50 = $35), Devon ($70 - $50 = $20), and Priya ($55 - $50 = $5) buy tickets, while Luis ($40 < $50) does not. Total CS = $35 + $20 + $5 = $60.
Diagnostic fallacy (Single-Buyer Truncation): $35 is only Maya's individual surplus; you must sum the surplus across all three buyers whose WTP exceeds $50.

questions.title: Consumer Surplus from a Linear Demand Curve
questions.prompt_template: The market demand for campus bike locks is given by the linear equation P = 120 - 3Q, where P is price in dollars and Q is quantity of locks. If the market price is P* = $60, what is the total Consumer Surplus?

hints.text: Find the choke price at Q = 0, then substitute P* = 60 into P = 120 - 3Q to solve for Q*.
Apply the triangle area formula CS = (1/2) x Base x Height = (1/2) x Q* x (P_choke - P*).

options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Omitted 1/2 Factor): Computing Base x Height = 20 x $60 = $1,200 calculates the area of a rectangle rather than the consumer surplus triangle.
Diagnostic fallacy (Slope-Division Omission): Failing to divide (120 - 60) = 60 by the slope 3 gives an inflated quantity of Q = 60 and CS = (1/2)(60)(60) = $1,800.
Diagnostic fallacy (Double-Halving Error): Dividing the triangle area by 2 a second time (or halving the height from $60 to $30) understates CS at $300.
Correct. Choke price is P_choke = $120. Solving 60 = 120 - 3Q yields Q* = 20. Height = $120 - $60 = $60, so CS = (1/2) x 20 x $60 = $600.

questions.title: Producer Surplus from a Linear Supply Curve
questions.prompt_template: Local bakeries supply artisan sourdough loaves according to the linear supply equation P = 10 + 4Q, where P is price in dollars and Q is dozens of loaves. At a market price of P* = $50 per dozen, what is the total Producer Surplus?

hints.text: Find the vertical supply intercept P_min by plugging Q = 0 into P = 10 + 4Q, and solve 50 = 10 + 4Q for Q*.
Compute the triangle area PS = (1/2) x Q* x (P* - P_min).

options_template.feedback: Correct. Setting Q = 0 gives P_min = $10, and 50 = 10 + 4Q yields Q* = 10. Height = $50 - $10 = $40, so PS = (1/2) x 10 x $40 = $200.
Diagnostic fallacy (Omitted 1/2 Factor): Multiplying Base x Height = 10 x $40 = $400 finds a rectangle area instead of the Producer Surplus triangle.
Diagnostic fallacy (Ignored Supply Intercept): Using full price P* = $50 instead of (P* - P_min) = $40 gives (1/2) x 10 x $50 = $250, erroneously assuming P_min = $0.
Diagnostic fallacy (Total-Revenue Confusion): $50 x 10 = $500 is Total Revenue, not Producer Surplus, because variable production costs were never subtracted.

questions.title: Computing Producer Surplus from Firm Revenue and Cost Data
questions.prompt_template: A neighborhood espresso bar sells 250 iced lattes in a morning at $6.00 per latte. The direct variable cost of beans, milk, cups, and hourly barista labor for those 250 lattes is $900, while daily fixed overhead (shop rent, utilities, and insurance) is $450. What is the espresso bar's Producer Surplus for the morning?

hints.text: First calculate Total Revenue (Price x Quantity).
Recall that Producer Surplus equals Total Revenue minus Total Variable Cost (before subtracting Fixed Costs).

options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Profit-as-PS Confusion): $1,500 - $900 - $450 = $150 is the café's accounting profit after paying fixed overhead, not its Producer Surplus.
Correct. Total Revenue = 250 x $6 = $1,500. Producer Surplus = Total Revenue - Total Variable Cost = $1,500 - $900 = $600 (which then covers the $450 fixed rent and leaves $150 profit).
Diagnostic fallacy (Fixed-for-Variable Substitution): Subtracting fixed costs ($1,500 - $450 = $1,050) instead of variable costs violates the definition PS = TR - TVC.
Diagnostic fallacy (Gross-Revenue Fallacy): $1,500 is Total Revenue before deducting the $900 in direct variable production costs.

questions.title: Solving for Competitive Equilibrium and Total Social Surplus
questions.prompt_template: A competitive market is described by demand P_d = 110 - 3Q and supply P_s = 20 + 2Q. At the free-market equilibrium (Q*, P*), what is the maximized Total Social Surplus (CS + PS)?

hints.text: Set P_d = P_s to find Q* and P*, then find both vertical intercepts (P_choke = 110 and P_min = 20).
Compute CS = (1/2) x Q* x (110 - P*) and PS = (1/2) x Q* x (P* - 20), or directly TS = (1/2) x Q* x (P_choke - P_min).

options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (CS-Only Partial Sum): $486 is Consumer Surplus alone ((1/2) x 18 x (110 - 56)); you must also add Producer Surplus ($324) to get Total Social Surplus.
Diagnostic fallacy (PS-Only Partial Sum): $324 is Producer Surplus alone ((1/2) x 18 x (56 - 20)); you must also add Consumer Surplus ($486) to get Total Social Surplus.
Diagnostic fallacy (Omitted 1/2 Factor): Multiplying 18 x ($110 - $20) = $1,620 omits the 1/2 factor in the triangle area formula.

questions.title: Calculating the Physical Shortage under a Binding Price Ceiling
questions.prompt_template: In the portable battery charger market where demand is P_d = 100 - 2Q and supply is P_s = 20 + 2Q (free-market equilibrium Q* = 20, P* = $60), suppose the government imposes a binding price ceiling at P_bar = $36. How large is the resulting physical shortage?

hints.text: Plug P = $36 into the supply equation to find Q_s, and plug P = $36 into the demand equation to find Q_d.
Remember that a shortage equals excess demand: Shortage = Q_d - Q_s.

options_template.text: 12 units
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Output-Contraction Confusion): 20 - 8 = 12 units is only the drop in quantity supplied (Q* - Q_s); it ignores the additional 12-unit surge in quantity demanded (Q_d - Q*).

options_template.text: 8 units
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Supplied-Quantity Confusion): 8 units is Q_s (the actual number of chargers produced and sold), not the shortage.

options_template.text: 32 units
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Demanded-Quantity Confusion): 32 units is total quantity demanded Q_d at $36; you must subtract the 8 units supplied to find the unmet shortage.

options_template.text: 24 units
options_template.feedback: Correct. At P = $36, supply gives 36 = 20 + 2Q_s -> Q_s = 8, and demand gives 36 = 100 - 2Q_d -> Q_d = 32. Shortage = Q_d - Q_s = 32 - 8 = 24 units.

questions.title: Computing Deadweight Loss from a Binding Price Ceiling
questions.prompt_template: A market has linear demand P_d = 80 - Q and linear supply P_s = 20 + 2Q (free-market equilibrium Q* = 20, P* = $60). If regulators impose a binding price ceiling at P_bar = $44, what is the resulting Deadweight Loss (assuming the available units go to the highest-WTP buyers)?

hints.text: Find Q_s at P = $44, then plug Q_s into the demand curve to find consumers' willingness to pay for the Q_s-th unit.
Compute DWL = (1/2) x [P_d(Q_s) - P_bar] x (Q* - Q_s).

options_template.feedback: Correct. At P_bar = $44, 44 = 20 + 2Q_s gives Q_s = 12. On demand, P_d(12) = 80 - 12 = $68. Vertical gap = $68 - $44 = $24 and lost output = 20 - 12 = 8, so DWL = (1/2) x $24 x 8 = $96.
Diagnostic fallacy (Omitted 1/2 Factor): Multiplying $24 x 8 = $192 computes a rectangle area instead of the DWL triangle.

Diagnostic fallacy (Truncated Vertical Gap): Using P* - P_bar = $60 - $44 = $16 instead of the full vertical gap P_d(12) - P_bar = $68 - $44 = $24 gives (1/2) x $16 x 8 = $64, omitting lost consumer surplus above P*.

Diagnostic fallacy (Shortage-as-Base Fallacy): Plugging the full shortage (Q_d - Q_s = 36 - 12 = 24) instead of lost trades (Q* - Q_s = 8) into the triangle formula overstates DWL at (1/2) x $24 x 24 = $288.

questions.title: Post-Tax Buyer Price and Seller Net Price with Unequal Slopes
questions.prompt_template: A market has linear demand P_d = 100 - 3Q and supply P_s = 20 + Q (pre-tax equilibrium Q* = 20, P* = $40). The government imposes a $16 per-unit excise tax legally collected from sellers. What price do buyers pay (P_b) and what net price do sellers keep (P_s)?

hints.text: Add the $16 tax to the supply equation (P_s_new = 36 + Q) and set it equal to demand to find post-tax quantity Q_t.
Plug Q_t into original demand to get P_b, and plug Q_t into original supply (or subtract $16 from P_b) to get P_s.

options_template.text: P_b = $56 and P_s = $40
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (100% Pass-Through Fallacy): Adding the entire $16 tax to the old $40 price ignores the upward slope of supply; sellers must accept a lower net price as quantity falls.

options_template.text: P_b = $52 and P_s = $36
options_template.feedback: Correct. Setting 100 - 3Q = 36 + Q yields 4Q = 64, so Q_t = 16. Buyers pay P_b = 100 - 3(16) = $52 (+$12 burden) and sellers keep P_s = 20 + 16 = $36 (-$4 burden), matching the steeper demand curve.

options_template.text: P_b = $48 and P_s = $32
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Automatic 50/50 Split Fallacy): Splitting $16 into +$8 and -$8 assumes equal slopes, but demand (slope -3) is three times steeper than supply (slope +1), so buyers bear 3/4 ($12) and sellers bear 1/4 ($4).

options_template.text: P_b = $40 and P_s = $24
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Statutory-Literalism Fallacy): Assuming sellers absorb 100% of the tax simply because they legally remit it violates economic tax incidence.

questions.title: Computing Government Tax Revenue from an Excise Tax
questions.prompt_template: Consider a market with linear demand P_d = 140 - 2Q and supply P_s = 20 + 3Q (pre-tax equilibrium Q* = 24, P* = $92). If the government levies a $20 per-unit excise tax, how much total tax revenue does the government collect?

hints.text: First find the post-tax equilibrium quantity Q_t by solving 140 - 2Q = (20 + 3Q) + 20.
Multiply the per-unit tax ($20) by the post-tax quantity sold (Q_t).

options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Pre-Tax-Quantity Fallacy): Multiplying $20 x 24 = $480 uses the pre-tax quantity Q*, ignoring the 4-unit drop in sales caused by the tax.
Diagnostic fallacy (DWL-as-Revenue Confusion): (1/2) x $20 x 4 = $40 is the Deadweight Loss triangle, not the government's tax revenue rectangle.
Correct. Setting 140 - 2Q = 40 + 3Q yields 5Q = 100, so Q_t = 20 units. Government Tax Revenue = t x Q_t = $20 x 20 = $400.
Diagnostic fallacy (Triangle-Factor Misapplication): Multiplying (1/2) x $20 x 20 = $200 erroneously treats the tax revenue rectangle as if it were a triangle.

questions.title: Calculating the Harberger Triangle Deadweight Loss
questions.prompt_template: In a market where demand is P_d = 110 - 2Q and supply is P_s = 10 + 3Q (pre-tax equilibrium Q* = 20, P* = $70), the government enacts a $15 per-unit excise tax. What is the resulting Deadweight Loss?

hints.text: Find the post-tax quantity Q_t (or use Delta Q = t / (b + d) with b = 2 and d = 3) to determine how many units were eliminated.
Apply the Harberger triangle formula: DWL = (1/2) x t x Delta Q.

options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Omitted 1/2 Factor): Computing t x Delta Q = $15 x 3 = $45.00 calculates a rectangle rather than the triangular Harberger deadweight loss.
Diagnostic fallacy (Tax-Revenue Confusion): $15 x 17 = $255.00 is the government's tax revenue (t x Q_t), not Deadweight Loss.
Diagnostic fallacy (Post-Tax-Quantity Substitution): Computing (1/2) x $15 x 17 = $127.50 mistakenly uses post-tax output Q_t = 17 instead of lost output Delta Q = 3.
Correct. With slopes b = 2 and d = 3, output drops by Delta Q = 15 / (2 + 3) = 3 units (from Q* = 20 to Q_t = 17). DWL = (1/2) x $15 x 3 = $22.50.

questions.title: Scaling Deadweight Loss When an Excise Tax Triples
questions.prompt_template: In a competitive market with linear demand P_d = 100 - Q and linear supply P_s = 20 + Q, a $10 per-unit excise tax generates a deadweight loss of $25. If lawmakers triple the excise tax to $30 per unit, what is the new deadweight loss?

hints.text: Apply the Quadratic Excess Burden Theorem: DWL(t) = t^2 / [2(b + d)], so multiplying t by factor k multiplies DWL by k^2.
You can also verify directly by computing Delta Q = 30 / (1 + 1) = 15 and DWL = (1/2) x 30 x 15.

options_template.feedback: Correct. Because DWL scales with t^2, tripling the tax multiplies DWL by 3^2 = 9: 9 x $25 = $225. Directly, Delta Q = 30 / 2 = 15 (leaving Q_t = 25 > 0), so DWL = (1/2) x $30 x 15 = $225.
Diagnostic fallacy (Linear-Scaling Fallacy): Multiplying $25 by 3 assumes DWL grows linearly with t, ignoring that both the tax wedge and the quantity contraction triple.
Diagnostic fallacy (Doubling-Rule Misapplication): Multiplying $25 by 4 applies the doubling-quadrupling factor (2^2 = 4) when the tax actually tripled (3^2 = 9).
Diagnostic fallacy (Double-Linear Error): Multiplying $25 by 6 (2 x 3) misses the exact quadratic relationship (3^2 = 9).

questions.title: Computing Post-Tax Consumer Surplus After an Excise Tax
questions.prompt_template: Return to the linear market P_d = 100 - 2Q and P_s = 20 + 2Q (pre-tax equilibrium Q* = 20, P* = $60, pre-tax CS = $400). If the government imposes a $16 per-unit excise tax, what is the new post-tax Consumer Surplus?

hints.text: Solve for post-tax quantity Q_t using 100 - 2Q = (20 + 2Q) + 16, then evaluate P_b = 100 - 2Q_t.
Compute the smaller post-tax CS triangle: CS_post = (1/2) x Q_t x (P_choke - P_b).

options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Pre-Tax-Inertia Error): $400 is the pre-tax Consumer Surplus before the $16 tax raises buyer price and cuts quantity.
Diagnostic fallacy (Unadjusted-Price Error): Using post-tax quantity Q_t = 16 with the old pre-tax price $60 gives (1/2) x 16 x ($100 - $60) = $320, forgetting that buyers now pay $68.
Diagnostic fallacy (Omitted 1/2 Factor): Computing 16 x ($100 - $68) = $512 calculates a rectangle area instead of the consumer surplus triangle.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Why Airlines Use Dynamic Pricing Algorithms
questions.prompt_template: At a uniform coach fare of $350, a last-minute business consultant with a $900 willingness to pay captures $550 in consumer surplus while a budget-conscious student with a $400 willingness to pay captures $50. Why do airlines invest heavily in dynamic pricing algorithms to separate these two groups?

hints.text: Think about what happens if an airline simply raises the single uniform coach fare from $350 to $600.
Consider how segmenting travelers allows the airline to capture more of the consultant's surplus without losing the student's sale.

options_template.text: Because the airline's marginal cost of carrying a business consultant in a coach seat is $500 higher than carrying a student.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Cost-Difference Fabrication): Both travelers sit in identical coach seats with virtually identical marginal service costs; the difference is in willingness to pay.

options_template.text: Because dynamic pricing eliminates producer surplus in order to maximize consumer surplus for students.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Objective-Inversion Error): Profit-seeking airlines use dynamic pricing to convert consumer surplus into additional revenue and producer surplus.

options_template.text: Because charging a higher fare to last-minute business travelers while keeping advance-purchase fares lower for students lets the airline capture more of the consultant's surplus without pricing the student off the flight.
options_template.feedback: Correct. A single high fare would lose the student ($400 WTP), whereas segmenting by booking flexibility lets the airline convert part of the consultant's $550 surplus into revenue while still serving the student.

options_template.text: Because under a single $350 fare, the airline suffers a deadweight loss from carrying the student.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Surplus-as-Loss Error): As long as $350 exceeds marginal cost, selling to the student creates positive social surplus rather than deadweight loss.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Interpreting Positive Producer Surplus Alongside Fixed Overhead
questions.prompt_template: An independent San Francisco café earns $600 in morning producer surplus across 300 cold brews, yet its monthly fixed bills (shop rent, utilities, and insurance) exceed its accumulated monthly producer surplus, leaving negative accounting profit. Economically, what does this distinction reveal?

hints.text: Separate the café's day-to-day operating margin (Revenue - Variable Cost) from its fixed lease obligations.
Ask whether shutting down immediately today would save the café from paying its signed monthly lease.

options_template.text: The café is losing money on every cup of coffee relative to the cost of beans, milk, and cups.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Variable-vs-Fixed Cost Confusion): Positive producer surplus ($600) proves revenue strictly exceeds direct variable costs; the loss stems from high fixed overhead.

options_template.text: Producer surplus and accounting profit must be calculated incorrectly because both always have the same sign.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Identical-Sign Fallacy): Because Profit = PS - TFC, a firm can simultaneously have positive producer surplus (PS > 0) and negative accounting profit whenever TFC > PS.

options_template.text: The café should immediately raise its cold brew price above consumers' choke price to cover rent.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Choke-Price Error): Charging at or above the choke price drives quantity demanded to zero, wiping out all revenue and worsening losses.

options_template.text: The café's daily sales generate positive operating cash flow (PS > 0) that helps offset unavoidable short-run fixed costs, even though total revenue does not yet cover all fixed expenses for long-run profitability.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Positive PS means operating reduces total short-run losses compared to shutting down (which would forfeit the $600 contribution toward fixed rent), though long-run viability requires PS >= TFC.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Distributional Trade-Offs of Long-Term Rent Control
questions.prompt_template: Cities such as San Francisco and New York cap annual rent increases to protect incumbent tenants from displacement. Which analysis best summarizes the long-run welfare trade-off predicted by the Chapter 4 price-ceiling model?

hints.text: Identify who gains from below-market rents and who bears the burden of reduced housing construction, condo conversions, and shortages.
Distinguish between transfers to incumbent tenants and the net deadweight loss from unbuilt or converted apartments.

options_template.text: Incumbent tenants who retain rent-controlled leases gain surplus, but landlords lose surplus, rental supply contracts via condo conversions and halted construction, and newcomers face severe shortages and deadweight loss.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Binding rent ceilings transfer surplus to lucky incumbent leaseholders while reducing quantity supplied, causing application lotteries, broker fees, and deadweight loss for excluded renters like students.

options_template.text: Every low-income renter in the city becomes strictly better off while total social surplus rises.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Universal-Benefit Fallacy): Binding ceilings reduce total surplus (creating DWL) and lock out newcomers and mobile low-income students who cannot find an available unit.

options_template.text: Landlords respond to capped rents by constructing more affordable apartments to make up the lost revenue in volume.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Backward-Supply Fallacy): Lower returns below marginal construction and maintenance costs discourage new rental supply rather than stimulating it.

options_template.text: Housing shortages occur only in the first month and vanish permanently once demand adjusts downward.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Shortage-Disappearance Fallacy): In reality, housing shortages typically worsen over time as buildings age, convert to condos, and fewer new rental units are built.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Anti-Price-Gouging Caps After a Regional Disaster
questions.prompt_template: After a major storm knocks out power across a region, demand for portable generators surges while shipping extra generators from neighboring states requires expensive rush freight (high marginal cost). If state officials cap generator prices at pre-storm levels, what economic outcome follows?

hints.text: Compare the capped pre-storm price against the elevated post-storm equilibrium price needed to cover rush shipping costs.
Trace the effect on out-of-state supply, local shortages, and deadweight loss.

options_template.text: Out-of-state suppliers still ship maximum quantities because their goodwill overrides marginal freight costs.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Costless-Supply Assumption): When capped prices fall below the marginal cost of emergency transport, suppliers will not ship additional units at a financial loss.

options_template.text: The cap acts as a binding price ceiling that discourages high-cost rush shipments, creating severe shortages and deadweight loss from blocked trades with desperate high-WTP households.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Preventing price from rising to cover higher marginal logistics costs shrinks Q_s below what emergency demand warrants, causing empty shelves and large DWL.

options_template.text: The cap guarantees that generators are automatically allocated to hospitals and households with the highest willingness to pay.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Ideal-Rationing Fallacy): Under a binding ceiling, excess demand is typically rationed by first-come-first-served lines or luck rather than highest urgency or WTP.

options_template.text: The cap increases total social surplus because it keeps generator prices low for everyone.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Price-as-Welfare Fallacy): Keeping price low on empty shelves destroys surplus; total social surplus falls whenever binding ceilings block mutually beneficial trades.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.topic: Rationing & Deadweight Loss Under Price Ceilings
questions.title: Why Real-World Price Ceiling DWL Often Exceeds the Standard Triangle
questions.prompt_template: In textbook geometry, the deadweight loss of a binding price ceiling is drawn as the triangle between Q_s and Q*. Why might the true deadweight loss in a rent-controlled apartment market be even larger than that textbook triangle?

hints.text: Check the implicit assumption behind the standard DWL triangle: which buyers receive the Q_s available units?
Think about what happens when scarce units are allocated by random lotteries or long waiting lines instead of going to the highest-WTP buyers.

options_template.text: Because the standard triangle forgets to include the rent payments tenants make to landlords.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Transfer-as-DWL Confusion): Rent paid by a tenant to a landlord is a transfer, not a deadweight loss.

options_template.text: Because landlords earn higher producer surplus under a price ceiling than in a free market.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Producer-Gain Error): Binding price ceilings strictly lower producer surplus by reducing both price and quantity sold.

options_template.text: Because non-price rationing (lotteries, waiting lines, and misallocation) can award scarce units to lower-WTP consumers instead of highest-WTP consumers, and time wasted searching destroys additional surplus.
options_template.feedback: Correct. The textbook triangle assumes the Q_s units go strictly to the top-WTP buyers with zero search waste; misallocation and wasted search time expand true deadweight loss beyond that minimum triangle.

options_template.text: Because binding price ceilings cause the supply curve to slope downward.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Slope-Inversion Fallacy): Price controls cause movements along the supply curve, not a reversal of its upward slope.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.topic: Efficiency versus Equity in Welfare Analysis
questions.title: Distinguishing Pareto Efficiency from Fairness
questions.prompt_template: A policy debate arises over whether an unregulated competitive market equilibrium should be modified to help lower-income households. What is an accurate economic statement about the relationship between Pareto efficiency and equity?

hints.text: Recall what Pareto efficiency guarantees about the size of the economic pie versus how the pie is distributed.
Ask whether an outcome that maximizes CS + PS necessarily looks fair to everyone.

options_template.text: Any Pareto efficient market outcome automatically achieves an equal 50/50 distribution of income across all households.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Efficiency-Equals-Equality Fallacy): Pareto efficiency says nothing about equal income distribution; a highly unequal allocation can still be Pareto efficient.

options_template.text: Economists prove that equity concerns are invalid whenever marginal benefit equals marginal cost.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Normative-Overreach Fallacy): Positive welfare analysis identifies efficiency and DWL, while societies legitimately weigh equity alongside efficiency using normative value judgments.

options_template.text: Redistributing income via price ceilings always improves both equity and Pareto efficiency simultaneously.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Free-Lunch Control Fallacy): Binding price ceilings distort production incentives and create deadweight loss, violating Pareto efficiency.

options_template.text: Competitive equilibrium maximizes total social surplus (Pareto efficiency), but it does not guarantee an equitable distribution—explaining why policymakers face real trade-offs between pie size and fairness.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Allocative/Pareto efficiency maximizes total surplus (CS + PS), whereas equity is a separate distributional judgment; effective policy weighs both goals and seeks less-distortive ways to help vulnerable groups.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Evaluating Political Claims About Who Pays an Excise Tax
questions.prompt_template: A candidate proposes repealing a $0.50 per-gallon fuel tax paid by drivers at the pump and replacing it with a $0.50 per-gallon excise tax legally collected from oil refineries, promising that 'corporations—not drivers—will now pay 100% of the tax.' How does economic analysis evaluate this claim?

hints.text: Apply the distinction between statutory incidence and economic incidence.
Recall whether changing who writes the tax check changes the final pump price paid by drivers.

options_template.text: The claim is economically false: shifting statutory collection from buyers to sellers leaves the tax wedge, output, pump price paid by drivers, and net refinery price completely unchanged.
options_template.feedback: Correct. By Statutory Neutrality, economic incidence depends on the relative steepness (elasticities) of demand and supply—not on which side is legally required to remit the check.

options_template.text: The claim is completely accurate because legal statutes determine who pays 100% of any excise tax.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Statutory-Literalism Fallacy): Markets adjust prices in response to taxes; refineries raise wholesale fuel prices so drivers still bear their exact same economic share.

options_template.text: The claim is partially true because taxing refineries eliminates deadweight loss even though pump prices still rise.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Seller-Tax Zero-DWL Fallacy): The Harberger deadweight loss triangle depends only on the size of the $0.50 wedge and the curve slopes, not on statutory assignment.

options_template.text: The claim is reversed: taxing refineries actually lowers the retail pump price paid by drivers below its pre-tax level.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Price-Direction Reversal): Taxing sellers shifts supply upward, raising—not lowering—the gross price buyers pay.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.topic: Empirical Policy Application: California Gasoline Tax
questions.title: Separating Tax Transfers from Deadweight Loss in Gasoline Markets
questions.prompt_template: California levies state excise taxes (approximately $0.54 per gallon, alongside federal taxes and fees) on gasoline. When economists evaluate the social cost of this tax, which impact specifically represents Deadweight Loss rather than a transfer?

hints.text: Remember that money paid by drivers and collected by the state to pave highways or fund BART and Caltrain is a transfer, not destroyed value.
Look for mutually beneficial trips or deliveries that no longer happen because of the tax.

options_template.text: The billions of dollars in tax revenue transferred from drivers to state transportation agencies to repair bridges and fund transit.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Revenue-as-DWL Fallacy): Tax revenue is a transfer from market participants to the public budget (the orange rectangle), not a deadweight loss.

options_template.text: The lost satisfaction and productivity from foregone weekend trips, canceled small-contractor delivery routes, and slower commutes that occur because the tax raises pump prices.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Deadweight loss is the lost social value from voluntary transactions that never occur (the red Harberger triangle), which neither drivers, gas stations, nor the state capture.

options_template.text: The pre-tax wholesale cost of refining crude oil into gasoline.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Production-Cost Confusion): Marginal production cost exists with or without a tax and is not deadweight loss.

options_template.text: The producer surplus still earned by oil companies on gallons of gasoline that continue to be sold.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Remaining-Surplus Confusion): Surplus earned on units that are still sold remains part of positive social welfare, not deadweight loss.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.topic: Optimal Tax Design & Quadratic Excess Burden
questions.title: Why Economists Prefer Broad-Base, Low-Rate Taxes
questions.prompt_template: Suppose a state government needs to raise a fixed amount of revenue to fund public universities and highways. Using the Quadratic Excess Burden Theorem (DWL proportional to t^2), why do public finance economists generally prefer a small tax rate spread across many markets rather than a very high tax rate concentrated on a single market?

hints.text: Compare the deadweight loss of one large tax rate (say 2t) versus spreading smaller rates (say t) across two identical markets.
Remember that doubling a tax rate quadruples deadweight loss in a single market.

options_template.text: Because a high tax rate on a single market generates zero deadweight loss once quantity reaches half of Q*.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Zero-DWL Threshold Fallacy): Higher tax rates strictly increase deadweight loss quadratically; DWL never drops back to zero as t increases.

options_template.text: Because small tax rates are legally paid by sellers, whereas high tax rates are legally paid by buyers.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Rate-Incidence Confusion): Statutory assignment has nothing to do with rate size, and statutory neutrality holds at any tax rate.

options_template.text: Because deadweight loss accelerates with the square of the tax rate, concentrating a high rate in one market creates disproportionately larger excess burden than levying modest rates across a broad tax base.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Since DWL grows with t^2, keeping t small across a wide base dramatically reduces total deadweight loss per dollar of public revenue raised.

options_template.text: Because broad-base taxes increase equilibrium quantity above Q* in every taxed market.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Tax-Expansion Fallacy): Excise taxes reduce output below Q* in taxed markets; broad bases simply keep the output contraction and DWL tiny in each market.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
