questions.topic: Elasticity, Tax Incidence, and Revenue Stability
questions.title: Comparing Excise Taxes on Inelastic Necessities vs. Elastic Substitutes
questions.prompt_template: Compare two markets with identical upward-sloping supply curves and identical pre-tax equilibria: Market X is an essential commuter fuel with very steep (inelastic) demand, while Market Y is a discretionary snack with very flat (elastic) demand. If the government levies the same $1.00 excise tax on both markets, how do the outcomes differ?

hints.text: Trace how much quantity drops (Delta Q) when a $1.00 vertical wedge is placed into a steep demand market versus a flat demand market.
Connect Delta Q to deadweight loss (1/2 x t x Delta Q) and connect steepness to who bears the larger share of the $1.00 wedge.

options_template.text: Market X suffers a much larger deadweight loss and a larger collapse in sales than Market Y.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Inelasticity-DWL Reversal): Because buyers in Market X have few substitutes, quantity contracts much less (smaller Delta Q), producing a smaller—not larger—DWL.

options_template.text: Sellers bear almost the entire $1.00 tax in Market X, while buyers bear almost the entire $1.00 tax in Market Y.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Incidence-Elasticity Inversion): The more inelastic (steeper) side bears more of the tax, so buyers bear most of the tax in Market X and less in Market Y.

options_template.text: Both markets generate identical tax revenue and identical deadweight loss because the tax rate is $1.00 in both.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Slope-Blind Tax Analysis): Even for the same $1.00 tax, steeper demand shrinks Q_t less, yielding higher tax revenue and lower DWL in Market X.

options_template.text: In Market X, buyers bear a larger share of the $1.00 tax burden, sales fall less, tax revenue is higher, and deadweight loss is smaller than in Market Y.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Steep (inelastic) demand in Market X limits quantity contraction (small Delta Q -> smaller DWL and larger Q_t -> higher revenue), while shifting most of the $1.00 price wedge onto buyers.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.topic: Comparing Excise Taxes and Binding Price Ceilings
questions.title: Policy Comparison: Excise Tax vs. Binding Price Ceiling
questions.prompt_template: Both an excise tax and a binding price ceiling reduce the quantity of units traded below the competitive equilibrium Q* and generate deadweight loss. What is a critical economic difference between these two interventions?

hints.text: Ask whether quantity demanded equals quantity supplied at the prices buyers and sellers face under each policy.
Also compare where the 'middle' rectangle of surplus goes under a tax versus under a price ceiling.

options_template.text: Under an excise tax, the market still clears without a physical shortage and the government captures tax revenue, whereas a binding price ceiling causes a persistent shortage (Q_d > Q_s) and raises no tax revenue.
options_template.feedback: Correct. An excise tax allows P_b to rise so quantity demanded equals Q_t (no lines or shortages) while raising revenue t x Q_t; a binding ceiling suppresses price, creating excess demand and non-price rationing.

options_template.text: A binding price ceiling raises substantial government tax revenue, whereas an excise tax produces a physical shortage.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Policy-Effect Swap): This reverses the defining features of taxes (revenue, market clearing at P_b/P_s) and ceilings (shortages, zero direct tax revenue).

options_template.text: An excise tax lowers the price paid by buyers, whereas a binding price ceiling raises the price paid by buyers.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Price-Direction Inversion): An excise tax raises the price buyers pay (P_b > P*), while a binding price ceiling lowers the legal price buyers pay (P_bar < P*).

options_template.text: Only a binding price ceiling reduces producer surplus; an excise tax leaves producer surplus untouched.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Tax-Immunity Fallacy): With upward-sloping supply, an excise tax lowers both Q_t and seller net price P_s, strictly reducing producer surplus.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Welfare Impact of Cutting an Existing High Excise Tax in Half
questions.prompt_template: Suppose a state cuts an existing high per-unit excise tax in half (from t to t/2) in a competitive market with linear supply and demand curves. How does this tax cut affect market welfare?

hints.text: Trace the effect of shrinking the tax wedge on Q_t, P_b, P_s, CS, and PS.
Apply the Quadratic Excess Burden relationship DWL proportional to t^2 when t is multiplied by 1/2.

options_template.text: Output increases, consumer and producer surplus rise, and deadweight loss falls by exactly 50%.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Linear-Reduction Fallacy): Cutting t in half reduces DWL by 75% (to (1/2)^2 = 1/4 of its original size), not merely 50%.

options_template.text: Output increases, both consumer and producer surplus rise, and deadweight loss drops by 75% (to one-quarter of its original level).
options_template.feedback: Correct. Halving t cuts both the height and base of the Harberger triangle in half, reducing DWL to (1/2)^2 = 1/4 of its prior level (a 75% reduction) while expanding CS and PS.

options_template.text: Output rises, but deadweight loss stays unchanged because the market is still taxed.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Binary-Tax Fallacy): Deadweight loss depends sharply on the size of the tax wedge, not merely on whether a tax exists.

options_template.text: Consumer surplus rises while producer surplus falls because sellers lose the revenue they previously collected from the tax.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Tax-as-Seller-Income Fallacy): Sellers remit tax revenue to the government rather than keeping it; cutting the tax raises seller net price P_s and quantity Q_t, strictly increasing PS.
